iconicAnchor.label: Death Jump — Eiffel Tower (1912)
iconicAnchor.creatorOrTradition: British Pathé; analysis by BFI Sight and Sound
iconicAnchor.whyCanonical: BFI's analysis identifies suspense in a subject placed at the far edge beside beckoning empty space and in the duration before the decisive act.

sources.title: Archives online: British Pathé’s Death Jump — Eiffel Tower (1912)
supports: Edge placement, empty space, duration, and delayed action can produce high suspense without visual spectacle.

sources.title: How 12 Angry Men works — in 25 frames
supports: Changes in framing, camera height, encroaching figures, and darkness can turn a static room into escalating screen tension.
